title: Wheat Ridge well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Wheat Ridge, median well depth is about 30 ft with a 10 gpm median yield. Learn what that means for drilling cost, water levels, and buying land.
h1: Water wells in the Wheat Ridge area
intro_html: If you’re looking at a home or small acreage around Wheat Ridge, Lakeside, or Applewood, the wells here look very different from typical mountain properties. Records within about 5 miles show a lot of relatively shallow Denver Basin and alluvial wells, but with a long tail of very deep holes. I’ll walk through what the local numbers say so you can budget realistically and know what to ask before you buy or drill.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Wheat Ridge
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Wheat Ridge, reported well depths cluster on the shallow side. The median total depth is only about 30 feet, and the middle half of wells run 20–70 feet. About 80% of wells are under 100 feet. That’s typical where alluvial or shallow bedrock can produce usable water.

The catch is the spread. The 90th percentile depth jumps up to 264 feet, and the deepest well on record goes down to 1,760 feet. Around 11% of wells are 100–300 feet, 7% are 300–600 feet, and 3% exceed 600 feet. A driller bidding in this area will usually assume something near the 20–70 foot range for many domestic and monitoring wells, but they know a smaller share of projects can turn into true deep Denver Basin holes if the shallow zones don’t cooperate.

sections.heading: Well yield here: how much water is typical
sections.html:
On production, Wheat Ridge-area wells look pretty solid. From the 407 wells that report pump tests, the median yield is about 10 gpm, with the middle half in the 7–14 gpm range. That supports a household and normal outdoor use for an exempt domestic well, as long as you manage irrigation sensibly.

Low producers are in the minority: only about 3% of tested wells come in under 1 gpm and 9% fall between 1–5 gpm. Two-thirds land in the 5–15 gpm band, and about 23% test above 15 gpm. That’s encouraging, but remember these are completed wells — dry holes and poor tests that were never finished don’t show up. Before you buy, compare the permitted use (domestic, irrigation, monitoring) to the yield; a 10 gpm monitoring well doesn’t mean your next domestic well on a different lot will match it.

sections.heading: Water table depth and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels around Wheat Ridge are generally shallow. Out of 161 measurements, the median depth to water is about 13 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 10 and 23 feet. That’s consistent with the mix of alluvial and shallow Denver Basin bedrock noted on permits.

By decade, median water levels were about 15 feet in the 1950s, 18 feet in the 1960s, then a spike to 95 feet in the 1970s, before coming back to around 14 feet in the 2010s and 11 feet in the 2020s. That 1970s jump likely reflects a different set of wells being measured, not a permanent drop. The more recent numbers don’t suggest a steady decline. Still, individual lots can be very different, especially where fractured bedrock controls water, so use nearby, recent wells in places like Fairmount or East Pleasant View as your best guide.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit history
sections.html:
Wheat Ridge and nearby spots like Edgewater and Mountain View have a long well record. There are 9,473 permits in the area, with 5,319 recorded as constructed and 5,423 reporting a total depth. Permit activity picked up in the 1970s with 664 permits, then really expanded: 1,532 in the 1990s and 1,766 in the 2000s. Even in the 2010s there were 1,180 permits, and the 2020s already show 484, with new permits being issued through 2025.

Most permits are either domestic/household (about 39%) or monitoring wells (about 42%), with smaller shares for irrigation and stock use. The drilling records are dominated by a few names: Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 2,573 wells, Adams Water Well Drilling on 211, and James Drilling Company on 123. When you evaluate an existing well, those permit records tell you who drilled it, how deep it goes, and what aquifer it’s in.

sections.heading: Expected cost to drill a new well here
sections.html:
The subsurface around Wheat Ridge is mapped as Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, with some alluvial along the drainage corridors. Typical drilling rates here run about $50–$70 per foot. At the area’s median depth of about 30 feet, the borehole itself pencils out in the $1,500–$2,100 range.

But the total project is more than just footage. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished domestic well in this area usually lands in roughly the $7,500–$14,100 range at that median depth. If your driller has any concern you might need to chase water deeper — into the hundreds of feet, toward the deeper Denver aquifer — get a per-foot price and a not-to-exceed depth in writing so you understand the budget risk.

sections.heading: Key risks: contamination, low yield, and siting
sections.html:
The numbers say most Wheat Ridge wells are shallow and produce well, but this is also a heavily impacted corridor. Within about 10 miles there are 588 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 175 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations, and 144 historic mine features. Those don’t mean your specific well is bad, but they do mean water quality testing for PFAS, metals, and solvents shouldn’t be skipped.

On the quantity side, about 3% of tested wells make under 1 gpm and another 9% are 1–5 gpm, so marginal supply is a real, if smaller, risk. Verify any older domestic well can still meet your needs, and factor in pump replacement if it’s been in service for decades. For new builds, leave room on the site plan for proper septic separation and access for a rig and service truck; even a 30-foot well needs room to work safely.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot near Wheat Ridge
sections.html:
For a Wheat Ridge, Lakeside, or Applewood property, start by pulling the DWR permit: check total depth, reported yield, static level, and approved use. With a median depth around 30 feet and many wells in the 20–70 foot band, a functioning existing well can be a real asset, but don’t assume it’s trouble-free — get a flow test and a complete water-quality panel, given the number of regional PFAS and cleanup sites.

If you’re buying raw land, talk to a local driller about nearby wells and depths; remember that a small share here reach into the hundreds of feet and beyond. Make sure the lot is eligible for a domestic exempt well under current rules or has an augmentation plan in place. Finally, lay out drive, house, wellhead, and septic early so you’re not forced into a poor well location just to make the site plan work.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Wheat Ridge, Colorado?
faq.a: Within about 5 miles of Wheat Ridge, the median reported well depth is around 30 feet, and the middle half of wells run between 20 and 70 feet. About 80% of wells are under 100 feet deep, but there’s a long tail: the 90th percentile depth is 264 feet and the deepest recorded well goes to 1,760 feet. A small share of projects here can turn into much deeper Denver Basin wells.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Wheat Ridge?
faq.a: From the 407 Wheat Ridge-area wells with pump tests, the median yield is about 10 gpm, with most wells between 7 and 14 gpm. Only about 3% of tested wells produce under 1 gpm and 9% fall between 1–5 gpm. About 66% land in the 5–15 gpm range and 23% exceed 15 gpm, which is generally enough for normal household use if the permit allows it.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping around Wheat Ridge?
faq.a: The limited static water level data in the Wheat Ridge area don’t show a clear long-term drop. Median depth to water is about 13 feet, with the middle half between 10 and 23 feet. By decade, medians were around 15–18 feet in the 1950s–60s, spiked to 95 feet in the 1970s, then returned to about 14 feet in the 2010s and 11 feet in the 2020s. That pattern points more to changing measurement locations than a steady decline.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Wheat Ridge?
faq.a: In the Wheat Ridge area, drilling in Denver Basin bedrock typically runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of roughly 30 feet, the drilled hole itself runs around $1,500–$2,100. By the time you add casing, pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete domestic well at that depth usually totals about $7,500–$14,100. Deeper wells will scale up with footage, so get a clear per-foot bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Wheat Ridge, CO?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well. The Wheat Ridge area has many mapped impacts nearby: 588 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 175 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations, and 144 historic mine features within about 10 miles. Those don’t automatically contaminate your well, but they are strong reasons to test for PFAS, metals, and common solvents, and to retest periodically, especially before buying a property.
